content: We have formalized a splay tree, including correctness and O(log n)-amortized time, using the standard sum-of-logs potential function in this PR. Notably, the definitions were designed to reduce symmetric cases. Comments/discussions are welcome!

Chris Henson said:

Antoine du Fresne von Hohenesche My main comments were to replace BinaryTree with docs#Tree and remove the BST structure.

Here is the reason why we want to bundle BST structure. Consider otherwise: 

theorem nlogn_cost [LinearOrder α] (n m : ℕ) (X : Fin m → α)
    (init : BinaryTree α) (h_size : init.num_nodes = n) :
    splay.sequence_cost init X ≤ m * (3 * Real.logb 2 n + 1) + n * Real.logb 2 n := (...)

This statement is correct but misleading: BinaryTree may not be a BST, and then the access sequence will be arbitrarily mapped to some node in the key, resulting in an arbitrary sequence in the BST that has nothing to do with X.

Now, let's fix this by adding (h : isBST init) into the statement. 

theorem nlogn_cost [LinearOrder α] (n m : ℕ) (X : Fin m → α)
    (init : BinaryTree α) (h : isBST init) i (h_size : init.num_nodes = n) :
    splay.sequence_cost init X ≤ m * (3 * Real.logb 2 n + 1) + n * Real.logb 2 n := (...)

Another issue: This hypothesis is redundant and should therefore be removed from the statement.

When the access sequence is structured, say sequential access, then it is important to have an isBST init as a hypothesis. For a general sequence, it does not matter.

Moreover, when users want to prove this statement, they need to repeatedly show that each time splays yields a BST, because we prove this for a sequence of accesses, not just one.

With the BST bundle, there will be no misleading statement, and users do not have to repeatedly reprove BSTness whenever they splay.
Happy to define BST as a subtype of binary tree if you prefer.

Sorry you are right. Updated my message above. I couldn't find them quickly enough. Anyway, IsBST is much simpler :

def contains (t : Tree β) (p : β) : Prop :=
  match t with
  | .nil => False
  | .node k l r => p = k ∨ Tree.contains l p ∨ Tree.contains r p

instance : Membership β (Tree β) where
  mem := Tree.contains

def IsBST [LinearOrder α] (t : Tree α) : Prop :=
  match t with
  | .nil => True
  | .node k l r => (∀ x ∈ l, x ≤ k) ∧ (∀ y ∈ r, k ≤ y) ∧ IsBST l ∧ IsBST r

In fact it might be simpler still with docs#Traversable.foldl. As requested, I will hold off on the PR until Sorrachai replies.

Also if you prefer, it's possible to define IsBST without this double-recursion with contains, if you define IsBSTAux (t : Tree α) (lb : Option α) (rb : Option α) : Prop which also accepts optional left/right bounds for the keys. Then t.IsBST := t.IsBSTAux none none, and the recursion is l.IsBSTAux lb k ∧ r.IsBSTAux k rb.

Also note that a tree is a BST iff its in-order listing is sorted. That's a much easier definition to work with.

That's the only case in which splay trees in particular and BSTs in general make sense. If you have a partial order, then during your search you might reach a node which you can't compare your element with. In particular for this PR, its BST search as implemented now will fail to find elements in the tree if this happens.

One remaining item that I want to discuss is this:

How should we define

∀ x ∈ T, P x

where T is a binary tree.

Option 1: via defining a membership instance.
Option 2: Just fold it.
Option 3: use ForAllTree.

In my opinion, ForAllTree is the best option for BST because (1) it just performs a simple in-order traversal. It is clean, efficient, and easy to reason about.

Looking at option (1): When you define membership, then you have a double recursion issue. I look up each element, check it, throw it away, then look up the next. Very awkward.

Looking at option (2): fold is a complicated way to perform pre-order traversal. In BST, I prefer in-order traversal.
In addition, a binary tree is more complicated than a list so the meaning of ∀ x ∈ T, P x is ambiguous.

so the meaning of ∀ x ∈ T, P x is ambiguous.

What is ambiguous about it? What interpretation other than "every descendant of T satisfies P" are you worried about?
I guess you're worried about x ∈ T, meaning "x is a direct descendant of T"?

Yes, but also in an operational sense, ∀ x ∈ T, P x can be implemented in many ways: repeatedly look up an element x and check P x (option 1), or traverse T into a list and perform a list lookup, or directly traverse the tree and check. When I say traverse, there are 3 options (preorder, inorder, postorder). I prefer an interpretation that yields efficient implementation and ergonomic design (option 3).

We pushed the fixes from the review and it's green now. In short, we removed the BST structure and BSTAPI, split into Basic/Correctness/Complexity modules, cost is ℕ instead of ℝ, plus docstrings and lint fixes.
